summary:
MARS Explorer 

From Martian Data to Exploration Decisions

MARS Explorer is an interactive planetary GIS prototype developed by GEOuy that transforms NASA and USGS scientific datasets into geographic information for exploring Jezero Crater on Mars.

The project integrates CTX orbital imagery and elevation models from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, USGS geological mapping, and THEMIS daytime and nighttime infrared observations from NASA's Mars Odyssey.

Using QGIS, GDAL, and Python, these datasets are reprojected, aligned, and processed to generate terrain slope, ruggedness (TRI), and numerical grids for geographic analysis.

The application provides interactive 2D/3D exploration, terrain inspection, elevation profiles, and multi-stop mission planning. An experimental A* algorithm compares shortest traversable and terrain-aware routes using slope and ruggedness. THEMIS imagery adds complementary infrared context without implying calibrated temperatures.

MARS Explorer demonstrates how integrating and processing NASA scientific data can support terrain interpretation, route comparison, and exploration decisions.

From scientific observations to meaningful exploration insights.
details:
MARS Explorer — Intelligent Terrain & Mission Planner

Team: GEOuy
Challenge: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

The Problem

Exploring Mars requires understanding its terrain, geological characteristics, topographic obstacles, and environmental conditions before selecting scientific destinations or planning exploration missions.

NASA and its scientific partners provide extensive planetary datasets obtained from orbital missions, surface exploration, and geological research. However, these datasets are distributed across different instruments, formats, coordinate reference systems, and spatial resolutions.

Transforming these independent observations into coherent geographic information is a fundamental challenge for planetary exploration.

A satellite image can reveal surface features, but it does not directly explain terrain elevation or ruggedness. A digital elevation model provides topographic information, but additional processing is required to identify slopes, evaluate possible routes, and understand their characteristics.

The challenge is not simply accessing Martian data, but integrating, processing, and interpreting it to support exploration decisions.

Our Solution

MARS Explorer is an interactive planetary Geographic Information System (GIS) developed by GEOuy to demonstrate how NASA and USGS scientific datasets can be transformed into tools for investigating and planning exploration missions on Mars.

Focused on Jezero Crater, the landing region of NASA's Perseverance rover, the application combines orbital imagery, digital elevation data, geological mapping, and infrared observations within a unified 2D and 3D environment.

Rather than displaying independent datasets, MARS Explorer processes and connects them to enable terrain inspection, topographic analysis, scientific mission planning, route comparison, and environmental exploration.

Our approach follows a clear workflow: scientific data → geospatial processing → terrain analysis → exploration decisions.

Scientific Data Integration and Processing

The scientific foundation of MARS Explorer is the integration of publicly available planetary datasets from NASA missions and USGS research products.

NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter — CTX

CTX orbital imagery provides detailed visual information about the surface of Jezero Crater.

The project uses a 5-meter orthomosaic as a cartographic reference and a 20-meter digital elevation model (DEM) as the primary source for topographic analysis.

The elevation data is processed to derive terrain slope and Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI), which describe aspects of surface inclination and roughness.

These derived datasets support elevation profiles, terrain inspection, three-dimensional visualization, and experimental route evaluation.

USGS — Geological Map of Jezero Crater

The geological information from USGS SIM 3464 provides scientific context about mapped surface units.

The original cartography is transformed, simplified, and adapted for interactive visualization, allowing users to investigate geological features alongside topographic and orbital information.

NASA Mars Odyssey — THEMIS

Daytime and nighttime THEMIS infrared mosaics provide additional observations of the Martian surface.

The datasets are processed and aligned with the application's geographic reference system.

MARS Explorer uses these images to compare infrared image-intensity patterns and available coverage along exploration routes.

The image values are treated as qualitative digital numbers (DN), not as directly measured surface temperatures.

Geospatial Processing Workflow

QGIS, GDAL, and Python are used to prepare and transform these heterogeneous datasets.

The workflow includes:

  • Working with a Mars-specific coordinate reference system.
  • Reprojecting and aligning planetary raster and vector datasets.
  • Deriving slope and terrain ruggedness from elevation data.
  • Optimizing scientific layers for interactive web visualization.
  • Exporting numerical terrain grids for geographic analysis and route calculations.
  • Preparing elevation, geological, and infrared information for inspection and comparison.

This processing converts independently published scientific resources into a consistent geographic environment suitable for interactive exploration.

From Scientific Data to Exploration Decisions

MARS Explorer demonstrates how processed planetary data can support several complementary analytical workflows.

Scientific terrain exploration: Users inspect orbital imagery, elevation, slope, ruggedness, geological units, and infrared observations through interactive map layers and a terrain inspector.

2D and 3D terrain interpretation: A digital elevation model supports three-dimensional reconstruction of Jezero Crater, helping users interpret surface morphology and elevation differences.

Experimental route planning: An A* pathfinding algorithm compares shortest traversable routes with terrain-aware alternatives that incorporate slope and ruggedness into their calculation costs.

Mission planning: Users can create scientific destinations, organize multi-stop itineraries, compare route alternatives, and save exploration scenarios.

Topographic analysis: Elevation profiles can be generated along calculated routes or independently drawn lines, allowing investigation beyond mission planning.

Environmental exploration: THEMIS daytime and nighttime infrared image intensities can be examined along selected routes as complementary scientific information.

Scientific communication: Mission reports and exports document exploration scenarios, geographic observations, route statistics, and terrain profiles.

Together, these capabilities connect scientific observations with interactive geographic analysis rather than treating the planetary datasets as isolated visual resources.

Innovation and Impact

The main contribution of MARS Explorer is the transformation of heterogeneous planetary scientific datasets into a unified, interactive exploration workflow.

The project demonstrates how GIS techniques can bridge the gap between accessing planetary data and using it to investigate geographic conditions, evaluate alternatives, and communicate scientific observations.

Its value lies in combining data integration, derived terrain analysis, exploratory route modeling, and 2D/3D visualization within an accessible web application.

MARS Explorer is an educational and research prototype, not a certified navigation system. Its route calculations depend on the resolution and coverage of the available data, as well as the assumptions and constraints of the terrain model.

By making scientific information more understandable and interactive, GEOuy aims to demonstrate the potential of geospatial technologies for planetary research, education, and future exploration planning.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Use of Super Intelligence

GEOuy uses OpenAI ChatGPT as an AI-assisted tool for technical development and project documentation.

AI assistance includes technical planning, code generation and debugging, English writing support for specialized technical terminology, and assistance in preparing project documentation.

The project owner defines the scientific objectives, selects and evaluates the planetary datasets, makes GIS and design decisions, and validates the implementation and results.

AI-assisted code and content are reviewed and tested before inclusion in the final project. Any AI-generated visual or audiovisual material will be identified as required by the competition rules.
